title: Sperling's partial report: the limit is reporting, not seeing

blocks.text: **Sperling (1960)** flashed three rows of four letters. In **whole report**, people named only about **4.5 of 12 letters** (roughly 37.5 percent). It is tempting to read that as the size of sensory memory, but that is the hard part: it is a limit on reporting, not on what was seen.
children: Whole report measures how much you can say before the image fades.

blocks.text: In **partial report**, a tone after the display told people which row to report. They got about **3.3 of 4 letters (82 percent)** whatever row was cued. Nobody could know in advance which row would be cued, so information about all the rows must have been available at first.

When the tone was **delayed**, accuracy dropped to about 1 of 4 letters, and by about 1 second it was near the whole-report level. So **sensory memory has a large capacity but fast decay**: most of it is lost within about a second unless attention selects it for short-term memory.

**Brown (1958)** and **Peterson and Peterson (1959)** showed three letters, then had people count backward by threes for 3 to 18 seconds before recall. The counting blocked maintenance rehearsal, so the task measures retention without rehearsal. The average curve falls with delay, which looks like pure **decay**.
children: The hard part is that the average hides what happened trial by trial.

blocks.text: On the **first trial**, recall was still relatively high at 18 seconds, because no earlier letters competed. By the third trial recall at 18 seconds was lower, and after many trials it was substantially reduced. The steep drop comes mostly from later trials, so the same delay did more damage when more earlier material had piled up.

That is **proactive interference**: earlier information disrupts remembering newer information. The pattern is evidence for interference, not only time-based decay. The effective duration of short-term memory is about 15 to 20 seconds, and rehearsal and interference conditions change the outcome.

title: Chunking and capacity: Miller, Ericsson and colleagues, Alvarez and Cavanagh

blocks.text: **Miller (1956)**, in The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, proposed that short-term capacity is about seven **units**. The hard part is the word unit: it can be a digit, a word, a number or a phrase, and a unit can hold different amounts of information. So seven is not a count of equally sized raw elements.
children: Capacity is measured in units, and units vary in size.

blocks.text: **Chunking** combines smaller units into larger meaningful ones. **Ericsson and colleagues (1980)** trained a student to a digit span of **79** by using familiar running times to organize the digits. **Chase and Simon (1973)** found chess masters recalled more pieces than beginners on real-game positions, but the advantage was greatly reduced for random arrangements. The gain comes from knowledge-based organization, not a bigger store.

**Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004)** used change detection and found visual capacity of about **three to four** objects, falling for more complex stimuli such as polygons and shaded cubes. Their emphasis is on the amount of information, not a fixed number of items, so seven should not be applied to every visual-memory result.

title: The modal model: three stores and control processes

blocks.text: **Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968)** modal model has three stores. **Sensory memory** briefly retains incoming stimulation for seconds or fractions of a second. **Short-term memory** holds about five to seven items for roughly fifteen to twenty seconds. **Long-term memory** retains large amounts of information for years or even decades.
children: The stores differ in duration and capacity.

blocks.text: The hard part is that information does not just march through the stores. **Control processes** decide what moves. Attention selects part of sensory memory for short-term memory, and **rehearsal** keeps information available and supports transfer toward long-term memory. Retrieval also sends information back from long-term memory into short-term memory, so the flow goes both ways.

Looking up a phone number shows this. The directory floods sensory memory, attention picks the one number, repeating it (**maintenance rehearsal**) keeps it long enough to dial, and enough rehearsal can store it in long-term memory. **Elaborative rehearsal**, linking new information to what you already know, supports longer-term learning, and **recoding** reorganizes information in short-term memory.

title: Working memory is storage plus processing (43 times 6)

blocks.text: **Baddeley and Hitch (1974)** proposed **working memory** as a limited-capacity system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information. Storage keeps information available, and manipulation works on it. The hard part is that both happen at the same time, in the same limited system, which is why short-term memory as a passive holder was too simple.

Multiplying **43 times 6** in your head shows it. First 3 x 6 = 18. You hold the 8 as the ones digit (storage) and carry the 1 over the 4 (an operation). Then 6 x 4 = 24, plus the carried 1 gives 25, and combining it with the held 8 gives **258**.
children: The 8 must survive while other operations run.

blocks.text: Do not say working memory only holds numbers. Holding the 8 is storage, and carrying, multiplying and adding are processing, so the answer depends on both together.

title: Brooks (1968): why the response mode matters

blocks.text: **Brooks (1968)** asked whether a response interferes more when it uses the same kind of memory as the information being held. People held something in mind and responded either by **speaking** or by **pointing**. The hard part is that the result reverses across the two tasks, so neither response mode is easier overall.
children: What matters is the combination of memory and response.

blocks.text: In the **sentence task**, people memorized a sentence and decided for each word whether it was a noun. **Pointing was easier**, because holding the sentence occupied the phonological loop and speaking the answers competed with it.

In the **F task**, people memorized an F, followed its outline and classified each corner as inside or outside. **Speaking was easier**, because holding the F used the visuospatial sketchpad and pointing to spatially arranged responses added a spatial demand. A task is easier when the held information and the operation use different types of short-term memory, which shows verbal and visual-spatial memory are at least partly independent.

title: Articulatory suppression, word length and phonological similarity

blocks.text: Three effects tell you about the **phonological loop**. The **phonological similarity effect** is confusion between letters or words that sound alike. **Conrad (1964)** found that seen letters were confused by sound, with E replaced by B more than by a look-alike such as F, so visual input is recoded into a sound-based form. The **word-length effect** is better memory for short words than long words (**Baddeley and colleagues, 1975, 1984**), because long words take longer to rehearse.

**Ellis and Hennelly (1980)** showed the same time limit with digits: Welsh-English bilingual children had a shorter digit span in Welsh, because Welsh number names take longer to say. Span reflects how much can be said in about **1.5 to 2 seconds**, not the values of the numbers.

**Articulatory suppression** means speaking while trying to memorize, which occupies the rehearsal process. Recall gets worse, and both the word-length effect and the phonological similarity effect are reduced. Short words normally win by being quicker to rehearse, and seen items are no longer converted into sounds, so sound overlap matters less.
children: Each effect points to speech-related rehearsal.

title: The central executive and the episodic buffer

blocks.text: The **central executive** is not a store for a particular kind of information. It directs and maintains attention (focusing, dividing and switching), suppresses irrelevant information, coordinates the sketchpad and the phonological loop, pulls information from long-term memory, and performs calculations. It is criticized as a **homunculus**, a little internal agent in charge of everything, because naming a controller does not explain how control is done.
children: A label for control is not an explanation of control.

blocks.text: **Miyake and colleagues (2000)** answer by splitting it into **updating** (changing the information currently maintained), **shifting** (changing the task or operation) and **inhibition** (suppressing information or responses that interfere with the goal).

**Baddeley (2000)** added the **episodic buffer** as a fourth component, so it belongs to the expanded model and not the original three-component proposal. It has a limited capacity of about four chunks and binds information from the loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. People can immediately recall about **16 words** from a meaningful sentence, more than their span for unrelated words, and some amnesic patients can immediately recall a just-heard story.
